hook.text: Elon Musk wanted cheap rockets. Experts said impossible. He asked: what do the raw materials actually cost? Far less.

buildup.text: First principles thinking strips away assumptions and breaks a problem down to its most basic proven truths.

discovery.text: Aristotle defined it first: a first principle is a foundational truth that cannot be deduced from any other truth.

twist.text: Most people reason by analogy: it has always been done this way. First principles thinkers ask why it was done that way.

climax.text: Start from what you know is true. Build up from there. Ignore how things are currently done—it might be arbitrary.

punchline.text: Strip to the studs. Build from what is actually true.

quiz.question: What distinguishes first principles thinking from reasoning by analogy?
options: It copies what others have done
It breaks problems down to fundamental truths and builds from there
It relies on expert opinions

hook.text: For decades, suitcase makers never added wheels.

buildup.text: Reasoning by analogy copies existing solutions.

discovery.text: In 1970 Bernard Sadow added wheels to a suitcase. Critics laughed. Within a decade every suitcase had wheels.

twist.text: Analogy is not always bad. Most daily decisions work fine this way.

climax.text: Ask: am I solving this from scratch or copying a solution? If copying, check whether the original was ever optimal.

punchline.text: Copying solutions is fast. But the original may never have been good.

quiz.question: Why did suitcase makers not add wheels sooner?
options: Wheels were not invented yet
They copied existing suitcase designs without questioning the fundamentals
Wheels were too expensive to produce

hook.text: Socrates never lectured. He just asked questions until his students realized their own beliefs contained contradictions.

buildup.text: Socratic questioning peels layers from assumptions.

discovery.text: The method works because bad assumptions hide under layers of habit.

twist.text: Socrates was executed for it. Powerful people disliked having their assumptions exposed.

climax.text: Apply Socratic questioning to your own beliefs. The hardest and most valuable target is yourself.

punchline.text: Keep asking why until the assumption breaks. That is the real foundation.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of Socratic questioning?
options: To win arguments
To expose and test hidden assumptions through persistent questioning
To show off knowledge

hook.text: A machine stopped. Why? A fuse blew. Why? It overloaded. Why? A bearing failed. Why? No lubrication.

buildup.text: Toyota invented the Five Whys. Ask why five times in a row and you move from symptom to root cause.

discovery.text: The first why reveals a symptom. The fifth why usually reveals a systemic failure that, once fixed, prevents recurrence.

twist.text: People stop at the first or second why because the early answers are easy to fix.

climax.text: Train yourself to push past the comfortable answer. The real fix lives deeper than the obvious symptom.

punchline.text: Five whys deep is where the real fix hides.

quiz.question: Why is stopping at the first 'why' insufficient?
options: The first answer is always wrong
The first answer reveals a symptom, not the root cause
You should always ask at least ten whys

hook.text: An architect was told a building had to be cheap, beautiful, and fast.

buildup.text: Constraint mapping lists every boundary in a problem: budget, time, physics, law, and human ability.

discovery.text: Once mapped, you see which constraints are real and which are assumed. Many 'impossible' limits are just convention.

twist.text: Airbnb faced the constraint that strangers won't stay in homes. They questioned it and built a billion-dollar company.

climax.text: List every constraint.

punchline.text: Map the walls. Many of them are just painted lines.

quiz.question: What does constraint mapping help you identify?
options: Only the budget limit
Which limits are real and which are merely assumed conventions
The fastest solution available

hook.text: Charlie Munger says: instead of asking how to be happy, ask what makes people miserable, then avoid those things.

buildup.text: Inversion flips the question. Instead of solving for success, list the causes of failure and remove them systematically.

discovery.text: Carl Jacobi, the mathematician, said it best: invert, always invert. Many hard problems become easy when flipped.

twist.text: A startup asking 'how do we get customers' might struggle.

climax.text: Inversion does not replace forward thinking. It complements it by revealing blind spots the forward view misses.

punchline.text: Flip the question. Avoiding failure is half of winning.

quiz.question: What does inversion do to problem-solving?
options: It ignores the original problem
It flips the question to reveal failure points and blind spots
It only works for math problems

hook.text: A team launches a product and it flops. Afterward everyone lists what went wrong.

buildup.text: A pre-mortem imagines the project already failed and asks: what went wrong? It is a post-mortem, just done in advance.

discovery.text: Research shows pre-mortems increase the ability to identify reasons for failure by 30 percent over standard planning.

twist.text: Pre-mortems overcome groupthink.

climax.text: Before any launch, gather the team and say: it is one year from now and this failed. Write down why.

punchline.text: Imagine failure first. Fix it before it happens.

quiz.question: How does a pre-mortem differ from a post-mortem?
options: It is done after the project succeeds
It imagines failure before launch to identify risks in advance
It only looks at financial data

hook.text: Michelangelo said he did not carve David. He just removed everything that was not David from the marble block.

buildup.text: Via negativa means improvement by subtraction. Instead of adding features, remove what is holding you back.

discovery.text: Nassim Taleb argues that removing bad habits improves health more than adding supplements. Subtraction beats addition.

twist.text: People naturally think in terms of adding. Studies show even when subtraction is the better fix, 80 percent add instead.

climax.text: Before adding anything to your life, work, or project, ask: what can I remove? The answer is usually more valuable.

punchline.text: Don't add more. Remove what does not belong.

quiz.question: What does via negativa recommend?
options: Add as many solutions as possible
Improve by removing what is harmful or unnecessary
Never change anything

hook.text: Munger says it is remarkable how much long-term advantage you get by consistently not being stupid.

buildup.text: Most people chase brilliance. But avoiding obvious mistakes compounds into extraordinary results over a lifetime.

discovery.text: In tennis, amateurs lose by making errors. Professionals win by forcing opponents into errors.

twist.text: Avoiding stupidity is harder than it sounds. Every bias, shortcut, and emotional impulse pushes you toward dumb choices.

climax.text: Keep an 'anti-checklist' of things to never do. Review it before big decisions. Avoiding disaster beats chasing genius.

punchline.text: Skip the brilliant moves. Just stop making dumb ones.

quiz.question: What does Munger's approach to avoiding stupidity emphasize?
options: Only geniuses succeed
Consistently avoiding obvious mistakes creates long-term advantage
You should never take risks

hook.text: NASA's O-ring failed in cold weather and Challenger exploded.

buildup.text: Failure mode analysis asks: how can each component fail, what is the probability, and what is the consequence?

discovery.text: You rank each failure by severity and likelihood. The highest-risk items get fixed first, not the easiest ones.

twist.text: Most failures are not dramatic single points.

climax.text: Map failure chains, not just failure points.

punchline.text: Map how things break before they break. Fix the chain, not one link.

quiz.question: What does failure mode analysis prioritize?
options: The easiest failures to fix
Failures ranked by severity and likelihood
Only the most expensive failures

hook.text: A company losing customers added a loyalty program. Churn continued. The real problem was terrible customer service.

buildup.text: Symptoms are visible effects. Causes are hidden drivers. Treating the symptom feels productive but solves nothing.

discovery.text: Root cause analysis forces you past the symptom.

twist.text: Organizations love fixing symptoms because root causes often require painful structural changes that leaders resist.

climax.text: If a problem keeps returning despite fixes, you are treating a symptom. Go deeper until the fix sticks permanently.

punchline.text: If the problem returns, you only fixed the symptom.

quiz.question: How can you tell if you've only fixed a symptom?
options: The fix is expensive
The same problem keeps returning despite the fix
The team disagrees about the solution

hook.text: Kaoru Ishikawa drew a fish skeleton on a whiteboard. Each bone represented a category of causes.

buildup.text: The fishbone diagram organizes possible causes into branches: people, process, materials, machines, environment.

discovery.text: By filling in each branch, teams discover causes they would have overlooked. Visual structure prevents tunnel vision.

twist.text: The diagram does not identify the cause. It maps the search space.

climax.text: Use the fishbone to brainstorm broadly, then use evidence to narrow.

punchline.text: Draw the fish first. Data picks the bone.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of a fishbone diagram?
options: To identify the solution immediately
To organize possible causes into categories and prevent tunnel vision
To assign blame to individuals

hook.text: A factory had 200 defect types. Pareto analysis showed that just five types caused 80 percent of all failures.

buildup.text: Pareto analysis ranks problems by impact. Fix the vital few and most of the damage disappears.

discovery.text: It combines the 80/20 rule with data.

twist.text: Teams often spread effort evenly across all problems.

climax.text: Before fixing anything, rank the problems. Attack the top 20 percent. That single filter saves more time than any other.

punchline.text: Fix the vital few. Ignore the trivial many.

quiz.question: What does Pareto analysis help you do?
options: Eliminate all problems equally
Rank problems by impact so you fix the most damaging ones first
Create a detailed timeline

hook.text: Ice cream sales and drowning deaths both rise in summer. Does ice cream cause drowning? Obviously not. Both follow heat.

buildup.text: Correlation means two things move together. Causation means one actually causes the other. They are not the same.

discovery.text: A hidden third variable often drives both. Temperature drives both ice cream sales and swimming, hence drowning.

twist.text: Businesses confuse this constantly.

climax.text: Before claiming cause, ask: is there a hidden variable? Would removing the supposed cause actually stop the effect?

punchline.text: Moving together does not mean causing each other. Find the real driver.

quiz.question: Why can't correlation prove causation?
options: Correlations are always random
A hidden third variable may be driving both correlated trends
Causation is impossible to prove

hook.text: A plane crashed not because of one error but because five small failures aligned at the same time.

buildup.text: James Reason's Swiss cheese model says defenses are like slices of cheese.

discovery.text: Disasters happen when the holes in every layer line up. One lapse passes through if every other defense also has a gap.

twist.text: Adding more layers helps, but only if the holes don't align. Redundant systems with identical weaknesses fail together.

climax.text: Design systems with varied defenses. Multiple independent layers where each catches what the others miss.

punchline.text: One hole is fine. Aligned holes are a disaster. Vary the layers.

quiz.question: When do disasters happen according to the Swiss cheese model?
options: When one big failure occurs
When holes in multiple defense layers align simultaneously
When there are no defenses at all

hook.text: Eating an elephant seems impossible. But the old riddle says: one bite at a time. Decomposition is that bite.

buildup.text: Decomposition splits a complex problem into smaller, manageable sub-problems. Solve each piece and the whole follows.

discovery.text: Software engineers do this instinctively. A million-line codebase is just thousands of small functions working together.

twist.text: The hardest part is knowing where to cut. Bad decomposition creates new problems at the seams between pieces.

climax.text: Cut along natural joints. Find the places where sub-problems have minimal overlap and clean interfaces.

punchline.text: Big problems are just small problems stacked. Find the seams.

quiz.question: What is the biggest risk when decomposing a problem?
options: Making the pieces too small
Cutting in the wrong places and creating new problems at the seams
Spending too much time on planning

hook.text: McKinsey consultants split every problem using one rule: mutually exclusive, collectively exhaustive.

buildup.text: MECE means every piece of the problem belongs in exactly one bucket, and all buckets together cover the entire problem.

discovery.text: Without MECE, you double-count some factors and miss others. The analysis looks thorough but has hidden holes.

twist.text: Perfect MECE is often impossible in messy reality. Aim for close enough. Even imperfect MECE beats no structure.

climax.text: Split your next big decision into MECE categories.

punchline.text: No overlaps, no gaps. Clean structure makes clean thinking.

quiz.question: What does MECE stand for?
options: Maximum Efficiency, Controlled Execution
Mutually Exclusive, Collectively Exhaustive
Multiple Estimates, Combined Evaluation

hook.text: A building's tenants complained the elevator was too slow. Engineers quoted $1 million for a faster motor.

buildup.text: The real problem was not speed—it was boredom during the wait. Mirrors gave people something to do. Complaints vanished.

discovery.text: Reframing changes the question itself. A different question leads to a completely different and often cheaper solution.

twist.text: Most teams accept the first frame they receive. 'The elevator is slow' is a frame, not a fact.

climax.text: Before solving.

punchline.text: Wrong question, wrong solution. Reframe first.

quiz.question: Why did adding mirrors solve the slow elevator complaint?
options: Mirrors made the elevator faster
The real problem was boredom, not speed, and mirrors solved boredom
People stopped using the elevator

hook.text: How many piano tuners are in Chicago? Enrico Fermi could estimate it in minutes with no data.

buildup.text: Fermi estimation breaks an impossible question into smaller guessable pieces: households, piano ownership.

discovery.text: Multiply rough estimates together and the errors cancel out.

twist.text: Google and McKinsey use Fermi problems in interviews.

climax.text: Practice Fermi estimation on any question.

punchline.text: No data? No problem. Decompose and estimate.

quiz.question: Why do Fermi estimations work despite rough guesses?
options: Each guess is perfectly accurate
Overestimates and underestimates tend to cancel each other out
They use secret formulas

hook.text: A client says: I need a faster horse. Go up the abstraction ladder: they need faster transportation.

buildup.text: Abstraction laddering moves between concrete and abstract. Go up to broaden options.

discovery.text: Most people stay stuck at one level. They solve the problem as stated without questioning whether the level is right.

twist.text: Going too abstract is also a trap. 'Make the world better' is too high to act on. You need to come back down to earth.

climax.text: Move up to find the real need, then move down to find the real action.

punchline.text: Go up to see options. Come down to take action.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of moving up the abstraction ladder?
options: To make the problem vague
To broaden the solution space and find the real underlying need
To avoid solving the problem

hook.text: A battery and a water tank look nothing alike. But both store energy and release it on demand. That is a deep analogy.

buildup.text: Surface analogies match appearance: 'this startup is the Uber of laundry.' Deep analogies match underlying structure.

discovery.text: Deep analogies transfer better. Understanding how water pressure works helps you understand voltage in electricity.

twist.text: Surface analogies mislead.

climax.text: When using analogies, ask: is the similarity structural or cosmetic? Only structural matches can safely guide decisions.

punchline.text: Looking alike means nothing. Working alike means everything.

quiz.question: What makes a deep analogy more useful than a surface analogy?
options: It uses more complex language
It matches underlying structural patterns rather than superficial appearances
Deep analogies always involve science

hook.text: Velcro was invented after a Swiss engineer studied burrs stuck to his dog's fur.

buildup.text: Biomimicry borrows solutions from nature. Shark skin inspired low-drag swimsuits.

discovery.text: Evolution is the longest-running R&D lab in history.

twist.text: Not all biological solutions transfer. Wings work for birds but not for planes at scale. Know when the analogy breaks.

climax.text: When stuck on a design problem, ask: has nature solved something similar? The answer is usually yes.

punchline.text: Nature already solved it. Look there first.

quiz.question: Why is biomimicry a valuable problem-solving approach?
options: All biological solutions transfer perfectly to engineering
Evolution has tested solutions over billions of years of trial and error
Nature is always simpler than engineering

hook.text: A Formula 1 pit crew can change four tires in under two seconds.

buildup.text: Cross-industry transfer takes a proven solution from one domain and applies it to a completely different one.

discovery.text: The key is spotting the shared structure: both pit stops and surgeries are high-stakes, time-critical handoff sequences.

twist.text: Industries rarely look outside their own walls. Hospitals study hospitals. Banks study banks.

climax.text: Deliberately study unrelated industries. Ask: who has solved a structurally similar problem? Import their method.

punchline.text: The best solution may come from a completely different field.

quiz.question: What enabled the hospital to learn from a Formula 1 pit crew?
options: Both use the same equipment
Both involve high-stakes, time-critical handoff sequences
Doctors are car racing fans

hook.text: Gutenberg combined a wine press and a coin punch to invent the printing press.

buildup.text: Far analogies connect domains with no obvious relationship. The greater the distance, the more novel the solution.

discovery.text: Research shows that people who solved problems using far analogies produced more creative and effective solutions.

twist.text: Far analogies are hard to find because your brain defaults to nearby, familiar comparisons.

climax.text: Build the habit: when stuck, ask what your problem looks like in biology, music, cooking, or sports.

punchline.text: The farther the analogy, the fresher the solution.

quiz.question: Why are far analogies more likely to produce creative solutions?
options: They are easier to find
The greater conceptual distance creates novel connections nobody else sees
Far analogies are always more accurate

hook.text: A CEO said 'our company is a family.' Then she fired 200 people. Families don't fire members.

buildup.text: Every analogy has a breaking point where the comparison no longer holds.

discovery.text: Stress-testing an analogy means asking: where does this comparison fail? What is different between the two situations?

twist.text: Bad analogies are not just useless—they are dangerous. They carry hidden assumptions that drive wrong decisions.

climax.text: Use every analogy but also break it. List three ways the comparison fails. That shows you the limits of the insight.

punchline.text: Every analogy breaks somewhere. Find the crack before it matters.

quiz.question: Why should you stress-test analogies?
options: Analogies are always wrong
Finding where the comparison fails reveals hidden assumptions and limits
Stress-testing makes analogies stronger

hook.text: A truck got stuck under a low bridge. Engineers debated cutting the bridge. A child said: let the air out of the tires.

buildup.text: Edward de Bono coined lateral thinking: approaching problems indirectly rather than through conventional logic.

discovery.text: Vertical thinking digs the same hole deeper. Lateral thinking digs a new hole in a different spot entirely.

twist.text: Lateral thinking feels risky because it abandons the obvious path.

climax.text: When stuck, deliberately generate absurd solutions. One in ten absurd ideas contains the kernel of a brilliant approach.

punchline.text: Stop digging deeper. Start digging somewhere else.

quiz.question: What distinguishes lateral from vertical thinking?
options: Lateral thinking uses more data
Lateral thinking approaches problems indirectly from a new angle
Vertical thinking is always wrong

hook.text: Netflix didn't invent movies. It substituted delivery. Uber didn't invent taxis. It combined taxis with smartphones.

buildup.text: SCAMPER is a checklist: Substitute, Combine, Adapt, Modify, Put to other use, Eliminate, Reverse.

discovery.text: Each prompt forces a different creative transformation.

twist.text: Most innovation is not invention from scratch. It is recombination of existing elements using exactly these operations.

climax.text: Take any product or process and run SCAMPER on it. At least two of the seven prompts will suggest something viable.

punchline.text: Innovation is rarely new. It is old things rearranged cleverly.

quiz.question: What does the S in SCAMPER stand for?
options: Simplify
Substitute
Systematize

hook.text: Dr. Seuss wrote Green Eggs and Ham using only 50 words after a bet with his publisher. Constraint forced brilliance.

buildup.text: Constraints narrow the solution space. A narrower space forces you to think harder and find more creative paths.

discovery.text: Twitter's 140-character limit spawned an entire new style of communication.

twist.text: Unlimited freedom often causes paralysis. Too many options overwhelm the brain.

climax.text: When stuck, add a constraint. Cut the budget, halve the time, or limit the tools. Creativity thrives inside tight boxes.

punchline.text: Tight boxes force creative escapes. Add constraints on purpose.

quiz.question: How do constraints boost creativity?
options: They eliminate all options
They narrow the solution space and force more inventive thinking
Constraints always reduce quality

hook.text: A brainstorming session produced 60 wild ideas. Then the team picked three and refined them. Two phases, one solution.

buildup.text: Divergent thinking generates many options without judgment.

discovery.text: Problems arise when teams mix the two. Judging ideas during brainstorming kills creativity.

twist.text: Most meetings default to convergent.

climax.text: Separate the phases explicitly. First diverge without limits: no bad ideas.

punchline.text: Create first, judge later. Never at the same time.

quiz.question: Why should divergent and convergent thinking be separated?
options: They use different parts of the brain
Judging ideas during brainstorming kills creativity and mixing wastes time
Only one phase is ever needed

hook.text: Archimedes struggled with a gold-purity problem for weeks. The answer hit him in the bathtub.

buildup.text: The incubation effect says stepping away from a problem lets your subconscious brain keep working on it silently.

discovery.text: Studies confirm it: people who take breaks between problem-solving sessions outperform those who push through without.

twist.text: The key is loading the problem deeply first. Without intense initial effort, incubation has nothing to work with.

climax.text: Work hard on a problem, then walk away. Sleep, exercise, or do something unrelated. The answer often arrives uninvited.

punchline.text: Load the problem, then let go. Your brain works while you rest.

quiz.question: What is required before incubation can work?
options: Avoid thinking about the problem entirely
Intensive initial effort to deeply load the problem into your mind
Simply waiting long enough
